entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Lev.19.1">Lev 19:1</reference> <div eID="gen1399" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1400" type="x-p"/> Holiness of Behaviour Towards God and Man. - However manifold the commandments, which are grouped together rather according to a loose association of ideas than according to any logical arrangement, they are all linked together by the common purpose expressed in <reference osisRef="Lev.19.2">Lev 19:2</reference> in the words, “<hi type="italic">Ye shall be holy, for I am holy, Jehovah your God</hi>.” The absence of any strictly logical arrangement is to be explained chiefly from the nature of the object, and the great variety of circumstances occurring in life which no casuistry can fully exhaust, so that any attempt to throw light upon these relations must consist more or less of the description of a series of concrete events. <div eID="gen1400" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1401" type="x-p"/> The commandment in <reference osisRef="Lev.19.2">Lev 19:2</reference>, “to be holy as God is holy,” expresses on the one hand the principle upon which all the different commandments that follow were based, and on the other hand the goal which the Israelites were to keep before them as the nation of Jehovah.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Lev.19.3">Lev 19:3</reference> <div eID="gen1401" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1402" type="x-p"/> The first thing required is reverence towards parents and the observance of the Lord’s Sabbaths-the two leading pillars of the moral government, and of social well-being. To fear father and mother answers to the honour commanded in the decalogue to be paid to parents; and in the observance of the Sabbaths the labour connected with a social calling is sanctified to the Lord God.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Lev.19.4">Lev 19:4</reference> <div eID="gen1402" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1403" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Lev.19.4">Lev 19:4</reference> embraces the first two commandments of the decalogue: viz., not to turn to idols to worship them (<reference osisRef="Deut.31.18">Deu 31:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.31.20">Deu 31:20</reference>), nor to make molten gods (see at <reference osisRef="Exod.34.17">Exo 34:17</reference>). The gods beside Jehovah are called <hi type="italic">elilim</hi>, i.e., nothings, from their true nature.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Lev.19.5-Lev.19.8">Lev 19:5-8</reference> <div eID="gen1403" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1404" type="x-p"/> True fidelity to Jehovah was to be shown, so far as sacrifice, the leading form of divine worship, was concerned, in the fact, that the holiness of the sacrificial flesh was strictly preserved in the sacrificial meals, and none of the flesh of the peace-offerings eaten on the third day. To this end the command in <reference osisRef="Lev.7.15-Lev.7.18">Lev 7:15-18</reference> is emphatically repeated, and transgressors are threatened with extermination. On the singular ישּׂא in <reference osisRef="Lev.19.8">Lev 19:8</reference>, see at <reference osisRef="Gen.27.29">Gen 27:29</reference>, and for the expression “shall be cut off,” Gen 17:14. <div eID="gen1404" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1405" type="x-p"/> Laws concerning the conduct towards one’s neighbour, which should flow from unselfish love, especially with regard to the poor and distressed.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Lev.19.9-Lev.19.10">Lev 19:9-10</reference> <div eID="gen1405" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1406" type="x-p"/> In reaping the field, “thou shalt not finish to reap the edge of thy field,” i.e., not reap the field to the extreme edge; “neither shalt thou hold a gathering up (gleaning) of thy harvest,” i.e., not gather together the ears left upon the field in the reaping. In the vineyard and olive-plantation, also, they were not to have any gleaning, or gather up what was strewn about (<hi type="italic">peret</hi> signifies the grapes and olives that had fallen off), but to leave them for the distressed and the foreigner, that he might also share in the harvest and gathering. כּרם, lit., a noble plantation, generally signifies a vineyard; but it is also applied to an olive-plantation (Jdg 15:5), and her it is to be understood of both. For when this command is repeated in <reference osisRef="Deut.24.20-Deut.24.21">Deu 24:20-21</reference>, both vineyards and olive-plantations are mentioned. When the olives had been gathered by being knocked off with sticks, the custom of shaking the boughs (פּאר) to get at those olives which could not be reached with the sticks was expressly forbidden, in the interest of the strangers, orphans, and widows, as well as gleaning after the vintage. The command with regard to the corn-harvest is repeated again in the law for the feast of Weeks or Harvest Feast (<reference osisRef="Lev.23.20">Lev 23:20</reference>); and in <reference osisRef="Deut.24.19">Deu 24:19</reference> it is extended, quite in the spirit of our law, so far as to forbid fetching a sheaf that had been overlooked in the field, and to order it to be left for the needy. (Compare with this <reference osisRef="Deut.23.24">Deu 23:24</reference>-25.)

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Lev.19.11-Lev.19.13">Lev 19:11-13</reference> <div eID="gen1406" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1407" type="x-p"/> The Israelites were not to steal (<reference osisRef="Exod.20.15">Exo 20:15</reference>); nor to deny, viz., anything entrusted to them or found (Lev 6:2.); nor to lie to a neighbour, i.e., with regard to property or goods, for the purpose of overreaching and cheating him; nor to swear by the name of Jehovah to lie and defraud, and so profane the name of God (see <reference osisRef="Exod.20.7">Exo 20:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.20.16">Exo 20:16</reference>); nor to oppress and rob a neighbour (cf. <reference osisRef="Lev.6.2">Lev 6:2</reference>), by the unjust abstraction or detention of what belonged to him or was due to him, - for example, they were not to keep the wages of a day-labourer over night, but to pay him every day before sunset (<reference osisRef="Deut.24.14-Deut.24.15">Deu 24:14-15</reference>).

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Lev.19.14">Lev 19:14</reference> <div eID="gen1407" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1408" type="x-p"/> They were not to do an injury to an infirm person: neither to ridicule or curse the deaf, who could not hear the ridicule or curse, and therefore could not defend himself (<reference osisRef="Ps.38.15">Psa 38:15</reference>); nor “to put a stumblingblock before the blind,” i.e., to put anything in his way over which he might stumble and fall (compare <reference osisRef="Deut.27.18">Deu 27:18</reference>, where a curse is pronounced upon the man who should lead the blind astray). But they were to “fear before God,” who hears, and sees, and will punish every act of wrong (cf. <reference osisRef="Lev.19.32">Lev 19:32</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.25.17">Lev 25:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.25.36">Lev 25:36</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.25.43">Lev 25:43</reference>).

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Lev.19.15">Lev 19:15</reference> <div eID="gen1408" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1409" type="x-p"/> In judgment, i.e., in the administration of justice, they were to do no unrighteousness: neither to respect the person of the poor (πρόσωπον λαμβάνειν, to do anything out of regard to a person, used in a good sense in <reference osisRef="Gen.19.21">Gen 19:21</reference>, in a bad sense here, namely, to act partially from unmanly pity); nor to adorn the person of the great (i.e., powerful, distinguished, exalted), i.e., to favour him in a judicial decision (see at <reference osisRef="Exod.23.3">Exo 23:3</reference>).

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Lev.19.16">Lev 19:16</reference> <div eID="gen1409" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1410" type="x-p"/> They were not to go about as calumniators among their countrymen, to bring their neighbour to destruction (<reference osisRef="Ezek.22.9">Eze 22:9</reference>); nor to set themselves against the blood of a neighbour, i.e., to seek his life. רכיל does not mean calumny, but, according to its formation, a calumniator (<hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §149 <hi type="italic">e</hi>).

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Lev.19.17">Lev 19:17</reference> <div eID="gen1410" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1411" type="x-p"/> They were not to cherish hatred in their hearts towards their brother, but to admonish a neighbour, i.e., to tell him openly what they had against him, and reprove him for his conduct, just as Christ teaches His disciples in <reference osisRef="Matt.18.15-Matt.18.17">Mat 18:15-17</reference>, and “not to load a sin upon themselves.” חטא עליו נשׁא does not mean to have to bear, or atone for a sin on his account (Onkelos, <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi>, etc.), but, as in <reference osisRef="Lev.22.9">Lev 22:9</reference>; Num 18:32, to bring sin upon one’s self, which one then has to bear, or atone for; so also in Num 18:22, חטא שׂאת, from which the meaning “to bear,” i.e., atone for sin, or suffer its consequences, was first derived.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Lev.19.19-Lev.19.32">Lev 19:19-32</reference> <div eID="gen1412" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1413" type="x-p"/> The words, “Ye shall keep My statutes,” open the second series of commandments, which make it a duty on the part of the people of God to keep the physical and moral order of the world sacred. This series begins in <reference osisRef="Lev.19.19">Lev 19:19</reference> with the commandment not to mix the things which are separated in the creation of God. “Thou shalt not let thy cattle gender with a diverse kind: thou shalt not sow thy field with two kinds of seed, or put on a garment of mixed stuff.” כּלאים, from כּלא separation, signifies <hi type="italic">duae res diversi generis</hi>, <hi type="italic">heterogeneae</hi>, and is a substantive in the accusative, giving a more precise definition. שעטנז is in apposition to כּלאים בּגד, and according to <reference osisRef="Deut.22.11">Deu 22:11</reference> refers to cloth or a garment woven of wool and flax, to a mixed fabric therefore. The etymology is obscure, and the rendering given by the lxx, κίβδηλον, i.e., forged, not genuine, is probably merely a conjecture based upon the context. The word is probably derived from the Egyptian; although the attempt to explain it from the Coptic has not been so far satisfactory. In <reference osisRef="Deut.22.9-Deut.22.11">Deu 22:9-11</reference>, instead of the field, the vineyard is mentioned, as that which they were not to sow with things of two kinds, i.e., so that a mixed produce should arise; and the threat is added, “that thy fulness (full fruit, <reference osisRef="Exod.22.28">Exo 22:28</reference>), the seed, and the produce of the vineyard (i.e., the corn and wine grown upon the vineyard) may not become holy” (cf. <reference osisRef="Lev.27.10">Lev 27:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.27.21">Lev 27:21</reference>), i.e., fall to the sanctuary for its servants. It is also forbidden to plough with an ox and ass together, i.e., to yoke them to the same plough. By these laws the observance of the natural order and separation of things is made a duty binding upon the Israelites, the people of Jehovah, as a divine ordinance founded in the creation itself (<reference osisRef="Gen.1.11-Gen.1.12">Gen 1:11-12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.1.21">Gen 1:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.1.24-Gen.1.25">Gen 1:24-25</reference>). All the symbolical, mystical, moral, and utilitarian reasons that have been supposed to lie at the foundation of these commands, are foreign to the spirit of the law. And with regard to the observance of them, the statement of <hi type="italic">Josephus</hi> and the Rabbins, that the dress of the priests, as well as the tapestries and curtains of the tabernacle, consisted of wool and linen, is founded upon the assumption, which cannot be established, that שׁשׁ, βύσσος, is a term applied to linen. The mules frequently mentioned, e.g., in <reference osisRef="2Sam.13.29">2Sa 13:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.18.9">2Sa 18:9</reference>; 1Ki 1:33, may have been imported from abroad, as we may conclude from 1Ki 10:25.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Lev.19.35-Lev.19.36">Lev 19:35-36</reference> <div eID="gen1423" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1424" type="x-p"/> As a universal rule, they were to do no wrong in judgment (the administration of justice, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.15">Lev 19:15</reference>), or in social intercourse and trade with weights and measures of length and capacity; but to keep just scales, weights, and measures. On <hi type="italic">ephah</hi> and <hi type="italic">hin</hi>, see at <reference osisRef="Exod.16.36">Exo 16:36</reference> and Exo 29:40. In the renewal of this command in <reference osisRef="Deut.25.13-Deut.25.16">Deu 25:13-16</reference>, it is forbidden to carry “stone and stone” in the bag, i.e., two kinds of stones (namely, for weights), large and small; or to keep two kinds of measures, a large one for buying and a small one for selling; and full (unadulterated) and just weight and measure are laid down as an obligation. This was a command, the breach of which was frequently condemned (<reference osisRef="Prov.16.11">Pro 16:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.20.10">Pro 20:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.20.23">Pro 20:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.8.5">Amo 8:5</reference>; Mic 6:10, cf. <reference osisRef="Ezek.45.10">Eze 45:10</reference>).
